debate.situation: You are the one who always initiates plans with a friend. Time together is lovely, but when you go quiet, so do they. What you know: the pattern, and that the meetings are good. What you do not know: why they do not initiate (busy, shy, assuming you like organizing, or less invested), and whether you want this friendship to change or just to feel more mutual. That unknown is decisive.

minds.title: The Voice Advocate
minds.concern: Speaking up early is how relationships get repaired instead of quietly drained.
minds.author: Albert O. Hirschman

minds.title: The Friendship Realist
minds.concern: Friendships differ in kind and shape, and not every imbalance is a defect that needs a talk.
minds.author: Michel de Montaigne

minds.title: The Gentle Interpreter
minds.concern: The story you tell about their silence may be wrong, so separate what happened from what it means before speaking.
minds.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen

debate.speaker: The Voice Advocate
debate.text: Yes, say something, and soon. Resentment grows quietly. If you stay silent, you will either keep carrying the effort until you are tired, or you will fade out without ever giving your friend a chance to respond. Voice is cheaper than leaving.
debate.author: Albert O. Hirschman
debate.basis: Basis: Albert O. Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Cheaper, perhaps, but not free. You are treating the imbalance as a flaw. Some people simply are not initiators, yet give full attention once together. You said the meetings are lovely. That may be the whole of what this friend offers, and it may be enough.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Gentle Interpreter
debate.text: Both of you are already telling stories. One says neglect, the other says temperament. What we actually have is one fact: when texts stop, plans stop. Why is a guess. Opening with a verdict about their care would turn a puzzle into an accusation.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, Difficult Conversations

debate.speaker: The Voice Advocate
debate.text: Fair, so speak without a verdict. But do not use that to stall. Your caution could become a polite way of never speaking at all. A light, curious remark now beats a heavy conversation after a year of silent tallying.
debate.author: Albert O. Hirschman
debate.basis: Basis: Albert O. Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Tallying is the real danger, and I grant that. But a talk can also be a test in disguise: say something, then see whether they rise to it. That turns a friend into a defendant. Some ties are better left unexamined if they are warm.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Gentle Interpreter
debate.text: Then the talk should not be a test. It can be a disclosure: I enjoy our time, I have noticed I am the one reaching out, and I am curious how you see it. That names your impact without claiming to know their intent.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, Difficult Conversations

debate.speaker: The Voice Advocate
debate.text: I like that, and it sharpens my view. Voice works best when it carries information the other person lacks. Your friend may have no idea the effort is lopsided. That makes speaking a gift of information, not a complaint.
debate.author: Albert O. Hirschman
debate.basis: Basis: Albert O. Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Or they know perfectly well and are content to be invited. Then your gift of information lands as pressure. So I would add a smaller experiment first: pause the texting for a few weeks, with no message attached, and watch. I go further than Montaigne here; he never proposed an experiment.
debate.author: Michel de Montaigne

debate.speaker: The Gentle Interpreter
debate.text: A pause is informative, but it is also ambiguous. Silence from both sides could just mean two busy people, and you would have learned nothing while privately keeping score. A pause works only if you can wait without reading the quiet as proof.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, Difficult Conversations

debate.speaker: The Voice Advocate
debate.text: Which is why I still lean toward speaking, though I now accept it should be light and curious, not a summons. We disagree about timing. I say speak first and then observe; the Realist says observe first and then maybe speak.
debate.author: Albert O. Hirschman
debate.basis: Basis: Albert O. Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the question may not be whether to speak but what you want the friendship to be and what the pattern means. One fact is clear, the other is a guess. Still disputed: whether to speak first (the Voice Advocate) or watch first (the Friendship Realist), and whether a warm but lopsided friendship is a problem at all. A possible self-reflection: does the imbalance bother you because of how it feels, or because of what you suspect it says about the friend?
debate.dependsOn: If the effort has started to feel like a burden or you notice yourself keeping score, a light, curious conversation becomes more reasonable, because unspoken resentment tends to harden. If the time together feels good and the imbalance does not weigh on you, doing nothing is reasonable, because it may simply be how this friend shows up. If you cannot tell what their silence means, a proportionate way to learn is either a few weeks of pausing your own initiating, or a casual remark such as: I have noticed I am usually the one planning, and I would love it if you suggested something sometime. Their response, over time, is the information.
